title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Before the workshop
Please finish these steps before the workshop so we can spend our time together on Quarto itself. They take about 15 minutes.
This setup builds on the Git workshop. It assumes you already have:

Git installed (on Windows, this gave you Git Bash)
A GitHub account
An SSH key connecting your computer to GitHub

Type every command below in a terminal: Terminal on macOS or Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or the terminal inside RStudio.

Step 1: Install Quarto
Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/download/ and run it.
RStudio comes with its own copy of Quarto, but please install Quarto separately anyway. The separate install works in any terminal, and it lets you control which version you have. You won’t break anything: RStudio will use your installed copy automatically.
When the installer finishes, close any open terminals and restart RStudio so they can find Quarto.


Step 2: Check your Quarto version
Open a new terminal and run:
quarto --version
You need version 1.9 or higher. Earlier versions can’t publish to Posit Connect Cloud from the terminal, which we will do in the workshop.
If you don’t see a version number of 1.9 or higher:

command not found: Quarto isn’t installed, or the terminal can’t find it yet. Re-run the installer, then open a new terminal and try again.
A version lower than 1.9: your terminal is finding an older copy of Quarto, often one installed for an earlier course. Run which quarto to see where that copy lives. Then download the current installer from the link above, run it, and check the version again in a new terminal.

For a fuller diagnosis, quarto check reports which version of Quarto you are running and whether it can find R and Python.


Step 3: Create a Posit Connect Cloud account
Posit Connect Cloud is a free service for sharing documents online. We will publish a report and a slide deck to it during the workshop.

Go to https://connect.posit.cloud/
Click Sign Up
Choose to sign up with GitHub, using the GitHub account you already have

The free plan is all you need. If you already have an account, you can skip this step.


Step 4: Create your workshop repo on GitHub
During the workshop you will build a small project about ice cover on Lake Mendota. Make a home for it on GitHub now.
In your browser, signed in to GitHub:

Click + (top right) → New repository
Name it mendota_ice
Choose Public or Private; either works
From the Add .gitignore dropdown, choose the R template
Click Create repository

Don’t skip the .gitignore. It tells Git to ignore the clutter that R and RStudio create (like .Rhistory and .Rproj.user/). It also gives the repo its first commit, so when you clone it, git push and git pull work right away.


Step 5: Clone the repo to your computer
On your new repo’s page, click the green Code button, select the SSH tab, and copy the address.
In your terminal, move to the folder where you keep your GitHub repos. We used ~/github in the Git workshop; use your own folder if it’s different. Then clone the repo, pasting your own address:
cd ~/github
git clone git@github.com:your_username/mendota_ice.git
Move into the new folder and look around:
cd mendota_ice
ls -a
.  ..  .git  .gitignore
You should see the .gitignore you created on GitHub, plus the hidden .git folder that holds the repo’s history.
That’s it. You’re ready for the workshop. We will start from this folder.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
Explain what Quarto is and how it works with R and RStudio
Write a report that mixes text and R code
Render it to a self-contained file and publish it online
Turn the same kind of document into a slide deck
Write a manuscript with citations and cross-references

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.2 What is Quarto?
Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system.



You write one plain-text file (a .qmd) that mixes:

Text, written in markdown
Code, in R or Python
A few options at the top, written in YAML




Quarto turns that file into a finished document:

Reports (HTML, Word, PDF)
Slide decks
Manuscripts and journal articles

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.3 R, RStudio, and Quarto
Three tools, three different jobs:











Tool
What it is
Its job




R (or Python)
A programming language
Runs your code: data, models, figures


RStudio
An IDE
Where you write code and documents


Quarto
A publishing system
Turns your .qmd into a finished document






You use them together: write a .qmd in RStudio, render it from the terminal, and Quarto has R run your code and builds the document around the results.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.4 What happens when you render
quarto render report.qmd






flowchart LR
  Q[".qmd<br/>text + code"] --> E["engine<br/>runs the code"]
  E --> M[".md<br/>text + results"]
  M --> P["Pandoc<br/>converts"]
  P --> O["HTML, Word,<br/>PDF, slides"]










An engine runs your code chunks: knitr for R, Jupyter for Python
Your numbers, tables, and figures are woven into the text
Pandoc converts the result to the format you asked for




The engine runs your code in a fresh session, not in your RStudio console. Remember this; it matters in the next unit.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.5 Why use Quarto?







The old way
With Quarto




Copy numbers from the console into Word, then they drift out of date when the data change
Text and code live together; numbers are computed every time you render


Rebuild the same figure for the report, the slides, and the paper
One source, many formats


Type citations by hand and renumber figures when you reorder them
Citations come from a .bib file; figure and table numbers update themselves


“How did I get this result?”
Rendering re-runs everything from scratch, so the document is the record


Binary files that Git can’t compare
Plain text that works with Git

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.6 A few quick notes
Quarto is its own program. Like Git, you run it from the terminal, and every command starts with quarto. It works the same whether you edit in RStudio, Positron, VS Code, or Jupyter.



It is not just for R. If your project uses Python, you can use Quarto the same way. Code chunks just say {python} instead of {r}.



Coming from R Markdown? Quarto is its successor. Most of what you know carries over, and your .Rmd files still work.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.7 Source vs. output











File
What it is
What you do with it




report.qmd
The source
Write and edit it; commit it to Git


report.html
The output
Read and share it; never edit it by hand






Quarto rebuilds the output from scratch every time you render, so any edits you make to the HTML will be overwritten.



To change the output, change the source and render again.

title: 1  What Is Quarto?
text:
1.8 Where we are
We have:

Defined Quarto as a publishing system, separate from R and RStudio
Seen what happens when you render
Seen why it beats copy and paste for reports, slides, and papers











ImportantNext up



Time to write one. Next we will build our first Quarto report about a Madison favorite: ice on Lake Mendota.
